t:
(a) In General.—Section 25C(g)(2) is amended by striking “December 31, 2017” and inserting “December 31, 2020”. 
    (b) Technical Amendment.—Section 25C(d)(3) is amended—
        (1) by striking “an energy factor of at least 2.0” in subparagraph (A) and inserting “a Uniform Energy Factor of at least 2.2”, and 
        (2) by striking “an energy factor” in subparagraph (D) and inserting “a Uniform Energy Factor”.  
    (c) Effective Date.—The amendments made by this section shall apply to property placed in service after December 31, 2017.

fable.w: This section only extends a tax credit's expiration date, updates technical energy-efficiency thresholds, and sets an effective date. It involves no consultation, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue, and no party outside the federal government takes part in any federal decision. There is no tempting contrary reading beyond the fact that taxpayers benefit from the credit, which is not participation.

opus.w: The section only extends the expiration date of the §25C tax credit and replaces 'energy factor' with 'Uniform Energy Factor' in the eligibility criteria. It does not require or allow rulemaking, public comment, hearings, consultation with outside parties, advisory bodies or a right to sue. The technical efficiency term may suggest an agency standard-setting process, but the statute itself sets the threshold directly, so no outside party is involved in any federal decision.
opus.b:
**Step 1: Reasoning.** A tempting reading is that "Uniform Energy Factor" suggests a federal efficiency standard, and setting standards often involves rulemaking. That reading fails because this section only changes tax code text. It extends the date in §25C(g)(2), swaps one efficiency measure for another in §25C(d)(3), and sets an effective date. It does not grant rulemaking authority or provide for comment, hearings, consultation, advisory bodies or a right to sue. No one outside the federal government takes part in any federal decision.

**Step 2: Label.**

qwen_chat.w: This section consists entirely of technical amendments to existing statutory provisions regarding tax credits for energy-efficient property. It changes dates and technical definitions (e.g., 'Uniform Energy Factor') but does not establish any process for public comment, consultation with outside entities, or advisory committees. The actors involved are implicitly Congress amending the law, which is an internal legislative act, not participation by outside parties in a federal agency decision.
qwen_chat.s: (a) In General.—Section 25C(g)(2) is amended by striking “December 31, 2017” and inserting “December 31, 2020”. (b) Technical Amendment.—Section 25C(d)(3) is amended— (1) by striking “an energy factor of at least 2.0” in subparagraph (A) and inserting “a Uniform Energy Factor of at least 2.2”, and (2) by striking “an energy factor” in subparagraph (D) and inserting “a Uniform Energy Factor”. (c) Effective Date.—The amendments made by this section shall apply to property placed in service after December 31, 2017.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that changing technical standards (like "Uniform Energy Factor") implies a rulemaking process that could involve public comment. However, the text itself only describes the amendment of statutory language and effective dates; it does not explicitly mandate a public comment period, hearing, or consultation with outside parties for this specific amendment. The definition requires the section itself to involve participation. Since this section is purely a technical amendment to tax code provisions regarding energy efficiency standards, and does not describe a process for outside input, it is "No".
